instructions:
Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 222 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool compared the draft with essays that students wrote on other assignments. Use its report when you revise:

Tone check against human essay writing (221 words). Distance from the human centre: 1.53 (1.0 is typical for a human text).
- net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean: 49.42 (per 1,000 words); most human texts are between -18.45 and 31.87. The ending is more upbeat than the rest of the draft by a wider margin than in human writing. Do not close on a lift the body has not earned.
- total charge, positive plus negative: 127.29 (per 1,000 words); most human texts are between 72.62 and 123.86. The draft is more emotionally loaded than human writing of this kind.
- charge under a negation: 0.0 (% of charge); most human texts are between 0.87 and 10.61. People negate more ('not good', 'isn't fair'). The draft states almost everything in the affirmative.
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences: 1.67 (1 = as if words were dealt at random); most human texts are between 0.63 and 1.65. Feeling is bunched into fewer sentences than in human writing of this kind.
Inside the human range: positive charge; negative charge; net charge; words that carry charge; charge after an intensifier such as 'very'; charge after a contrast word such as 'but'.
These are ranges, not targets. Change wording only where the change also makes the text more specific or more honest.

Draft:

Dear Principal,

I believe Policy 1 is the better choice: students should be allowed to bring phones and use them at lunch and during free time, as long as they are turned off in class.

First, phones are a safety tool. If a bus breaks down, practice runs late, or a family emergency happens, a student can reach a parent right away. Under a total ban, that call has to go through the front office, which wastes time when it matters most.

Second, a complete ban is hard to enforce and creates constant conflict. Many students will hide phones in their backpacks anyway, and teachers will spend class time searching for them instead of teaching. Policy 1 gives students a clear rule they can actually follow: phones off during class, free to use otherwise. People tend to respect a rule that feels fair.

Third, lunch and free time are when students need a break. Checking a message from home, listening to music, or looking up a homework question helps students relax and come back to class ready to focus.

Finally, learning to manage a phone is a real-life skill. Students will carry phones for the rest of their lives, and school is a good place to practice self-control.

For these reasons, I urge you to adopt Policy 1.

Sincerely,
A concerned student
